power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Research on social networking sites (SNS) and mental health has produced highly heterogeneous findings, often attributed to differences between platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok.
In response, cross-platform comparisons are increasingly proposed as a promising analytical direction, yet their actual conceptual and explanatory value remains unclear.

Rather than aiming to identify platform-specific effects, this Short Report critically examines whether a cross-platform perspective meaningfully advances our understanding of SNS-mental health associations.
To this end, we conduct a brief scoping review of quantitative studies that explicitly compare multiple SNS platforms within the same design (N = 14).
The review reveals substantial methodological and conceptual inconsistencies across studies, suggesting that platform-level comparisons alone rarely clarify observed heterogeneity.
We argue that future research would benefit from moving beyond platform labels toward a featureand affordance-based cross-platform approach that is more closely aligned with psychological theory.
Concerns about the impact of Social Networking Sites (SNS) on mental health have not diminished in recent years (1).
text.formatted: Concerns about the impact of Social Networking Sites (SNS) on mental health have not diminished in recent years <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: On the contrary, the emergence of new platforms such as TikTok has intensified public and scientific debate, particularly due to increased levels of content personalization and their widespread use among young people (2).
text.formatted: On the contrary, the emergence of new platforms such as TikTok has intensified public and scientific debate, particularly due to increased levels of content personalization and their widespread use among young people <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref>.

text.text: SNS are commonly defined as web-based services that allow users to construct a public or semi-public profile, articulate a list of connections, and access continuous streams of user-generated content (3).
text.formatted: SNS are commonly defined as web-based services that allow users to construct a public or semi-public profile, articulate a list of connections, and access continuous streams of user-generated content <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref>.

text.text: Through these features, SNS are likely to influence mental health by shaping everyday social interactions and by engaging key psychological processes, including social comparison and social support (4).
text.formatted: Through these features, SNS are likely to influence mental health by shaping everyday social interactions and by engaging key psychological processes, including social comparison and social support <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref>.

text.text: Despite these concerns, recent meta-analyses indicate that the overall association between SNS use and mental health remains weak and largely inconclusive.
This pattern has been observed both in adult populations (5) (6) (7) and in adolescents (8, 9).
text.formatted: This pattern has been observed both in adult populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref> and in adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9)</ref>.

text.text: Several explanations have been proposed, including methodological limitations, overestimation of effect sizes, and individual vulnerabilities (10, 11).
text.formatted: Several explanations have been proposed, including methodological limitations, overestimation of effect sizes, and individual vulnerabilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10,</ref> <ref type="bibr">11)</ref>.

text.text: One potentially important, yet still insufficiently examined, explanation for these mixed findings concerns the assumption that SNS constitute a homogeneous category (12).
text.formatted: One potentially important, yet still insufficiently examined, explanation for these mixed findings concerns the assumption that SNS constitute a homogeneous category <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: Outside the mental health literature, cross-platform approaches (13) have demonstrated that SNS differ meaningfully with respect to their digital architecture (14), usage motivations (15), and broader socio-cultural dynamics (16).
text.formatted: Outside the mental health literature, cross-platform approaches (13) have demonstrated that SNS differ meaningfully with respect to their digital architecture (14), usage motivations (15), and broader socio-cultural dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>.

text.text: However, research on mental health has long focused either on Facebook specifically or on aggregated measures of "social media use", thereby limiting insights into comparative effects between platforms (17).
More recently, some studies have moved beyond Facebook by examining individual platforms such as Instagram or TikTok (2, 18).
text.formatted: More recently, some studies have moved beyond Facebook by examining individual platforms such as Instagram or TikTok <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, platform-specific evidence remains too fragmented to support strong comparative conclusions.

In their recent meta-analysis, Marciano et al. (7) tested platform type as a moderator, but were limited to distinguishing between studies referring to social media use in general, Facebook use, or another specific platform.
text.formatted: In their recent meta-analysis, Marciano et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref> tested platform type as a moderator, but were limited to distinguishing between studies referring to social media use in general, Facebook use, or another specific platform.

text.text: No significant moderating effect was observed.
This could reflect the fact that such comparisons aggregate findings across different contexts and methodologies, thereby obscuring platform-specific effects.
This limitation underscores the importance of adopting a cross-platform approach in which multiple SNS are examined and compared within the same study, under identical methodological conditions (13).
text.formatted: This limitation underscores the importance of adopting a cross-platform approach in which multiple SNS are examined and compared within the same study, under identical methodological conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref>.

text.text: Rather than treating cross-platform comparisons as an empirical solution to inconsistent findings, this Short Report discusses their conceptual and explanatory value for media psychology research.
To support this discussion, we conduct a scoping review of quantitative studies that explicitly compare multiple SNS platforms in relation to mental health outcomes.
Scoping reviews are designed to map and characterize fragmented literatures, without aiming for exhaustive synthesis or effect estimation (19).
text.formatted: Scoping reviews are designed to map and characterize fragmented literatures, without aiming for exhaustive synthesis or effect estimation <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>.

text.text: Two research questions guide this review: We included all studies that (1) were quantitative, (2) were published in English in a peer-reviewed journal, (3) collected data from non-clinical participant samples, (4) assessed as independent variable usage time, intensity of use, frequency of use, or specific activities on at least two SNS, and (5) assessed as dependent variables a key mental health indicator (positive affect, negative affect, happiness, life satisfaction, depressive symptoms).

We excluded studies that (1) used qualitative designs or were systematic reviews, metaanalyses or intervention studies, or (2) did not distinguish between usage of different SNS platforms, or (3) examined messaging apps, smartphones, screen time or internet use, or (4) focused on other independent or dependent variables than those mentioned above.

We additionally screened the reference lists of included articles to identify further relevant records (19).
text.formatted: We additionally screened the reference lists of included articles to identify further relevant records <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>.

text.formatted: This search process resulted in the inclusion of 14 papers, as summarized in the PRISMA flow diagram (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>).

text.text: Following data extraction, all included studies were systematically coded using a standardized data extraction table.

Each study was coded for (1) SNS platforms examined, (2) study design, (3) sample characteristics, (4) measures of SNS use, (5) mental health outcomes, and (6) the direction and nature of reported associations, including the presence of mediating or moderating variables.
When papers reported multiple studies, each study was coded separately.

The obtained set of papers is relatively recent with the first study conducted in 2018 (22) and over 75% of the studies were published on or after 2020.

text.text: The number of platforms compared ranges from two to seven (mean = 3.7, median = 3.5).
The following SNS were included in at least two articles: Facebook, Instagram, Twitter (X), LinkedIn, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube.

The design of studies was 50% cross-sectional (n = 7), but there were also four longitudinal two-wave studies 1 (22) (23) (24) (25), one experimental study (26) and two experience sampling studies (27, 28).

text.text: SNS use was measured via self-report in the majority of studies (85.71%), with only one study employing an objective measure (27).

text.text: Most studies assessed SNS usage as daily time spent on the platform or frequency of use, but several studies also distinguished between passive and active SNS usages (12, 26, (29) (30) (31) following The (Extended) Active-Passive Model (32,33).

text.text: Finally, while most studies focused on adults, two studies involved adolescent samples (25, 34).
text.formatted: Finally, while most studies focused on adults, two studies involved adolescent samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">34)</ref>.

text.text: The samples were geographically diverse (Saudi Arabia, Korea, Germany, Japan, Belgium, Australia, United-States, Greece, Swiss, and France).
As summarized in Table 1, associations between SNS use and mental health were highly inconsistent across studies and platforms.
text.formatted: As summarized in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>, associations between SNS use and mental health were highly inconsistent across studies and platforms.

text.text: No platform showed a stable pattern of positive or negative associations with mental health outcomes.

Instead, the same platform was often associated with positive, negative, or null effects depending on the presence of mediating processes (e.g., social comparison, social support, information overload), moderating variables (e.g., age, gender), and measurement strategies (e.g., usage types: active vs. passive).
Facebook illustrates this variability particularly well.

Several studies found no association with mental health (22, 23, 25, 26, 30, 35), but two studies revealed a positive association when social support was considered as a mediator (29) and age as a moderator (31).

text.text: Other studies have also shown a negative association of Facebook use with mental health (27, 28, 36), particularly when social comparison was a mediator (12, 24).

text.text: Importantly, this pattern of mixed findings was found for all other platforms (Table 1).
text.formatted: Importantly, this pattern of mixed findings was found for all other platforms (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: The aim of this research was to examine whether a cross-platform perspective constitutes a useful analytical direction for understanding associations between SNS use and mental health (12).
text.formatted: The aim of this research was to examine whether a cross-platform perspective constitutes a useful analytical direction for understanding associations between SNS use and mental health <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: Rather than providing definitive conclusions, the goal was to assess whether this perspective helps to structure and interpret an increasingly heterogeneous literature.

In response to RQ1, the results indicate that cross-platform research in the mental health domain remains relatively recent, with most studies published from 2018 onward, despite the fact that many major SNS platforms had already been established for several years.

Most studies focused on Facebook and Instagram, whereas other platforms such as Snapchat or YouTube were only rarely examined, suggesting that cross-platform approaches do not necessarily translate into broader platform inclusivity.
Methodologically, the literature was heterogeneous, with a predominance of self-report measures but also the inclusion of experimental and longitudinal designs (17).
text.formatted: Methodologically, the literature was heterogeneous, with a predominance of self-report measures but also the inclusion of experimental and longitudinal designs <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, relatively few studies focused on adolescents, despite the fact that young people are often at the centre of public and scientific debates regarding SNSrelated mental health risks (10).
text.formatted: Notably, relatively few studies focused on adolescents, despite the fact that young people are often at the centre of public and scientific debates regarding SNSrelated mental health risks <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref>.

text.text: In response to RQ2, the findings suggest that comparing platforms per se does not automatically lead to clearer or more consistent insights into the relationship between SNS use and mental health.
Importantly, this does not imply that a cross-platform perspective lacks value.
Rather, it highlights the limitations of platform-level comparisons as an explanatory strategy.
Two challenges help explain why platform-level comparisons often yield limited interpretive clarity.
First, the literature continues to suffer from a lack of shared methodological standards, including validated measures of SNS use and sufficiently robust study designs.
This limitation extends beyond cross-platform research to the field more broadly (5).
text.formatted: This limitation extends beyond cross-platform research to the field more broadly <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: Second, SNS platforms are dynamic and continuously evolving, giving rise to a substantial "moving-target" problem (37).
As a result, studies conducted at different time points may capture qualitatively different platform environments, even when nominally examining the same SNS.

From this perspective, cross-platform comparisons may be most useful as an initial, necessary step, allowing researchers to establish whether associations with mental health differ across platforms at all.
However, once such differences are observed, platform labels alone provide limited explanatory power.
Differences in observed associations are likely to reflect variation in platform features, affordances, usage norms, and algorithms, rather than the platform as a discrete entity.
Accordingly, future cross-platform research should shift its unit of analysis away from platforms as such and toward the underlying features and affordances that characterize different SNS.
To understand differential effects of SNS on mental health, it is insufficient to state that one platform is more harmful or beneficial than another.

Rather, differences must be explained in terms of specific characteristics (e.g., visibility, personalization, availability of information, connection mode) that may activate distinct psychological processes.

For example, features such as anonymity may increase the risk of bullying, highly visual environments may amplify body image concerns, and design elements that promote continuous scrolling may be more strongly associated with attentional difficulties (e.g., 38).
A feature-based cross-platform approach may help mitigate the moving-target problem, as core affordances often persist even as platforms evolve, rebrand, or modify specific interface elements.
Integrating insights from existing cross-platform frameworks in media and communication research (e.g., 13) could help identify which platform features are most relevant for mental health research.

From a broader perspective, such an approach could also support more informed policy discussions by enabling anticipation of potential mental health risks associated with emerging platform features, rather than reacting to platforms only after they have become widespread (39).
text.formatted: From a broader perspective, such an approach could also support more informed policy discussions by enabling anticipation of potential mental health risks associated with emerging platform features, rather than reacting to platforms only after they have become widespread <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(39)</ref>.

text.text: The present research has limitations that are inherent to its exploratory aim and to the current state of the literature.

First, as a scoping review, it was not intended to provide a systematic or exhaustive synthesis, nor to estimate effect sizes, but rather to map existing quantitative research and assess the analytical value of a cross-platform perspective (19).
text.formatted: First, as a scoping review, it was not intended to provide a systematic or exhaustive synthesis, nor to estimate effect sizes, but rather to map existing quantitative research and assess the analytical value of a cross-platform perspective <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(19)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the set of platforms examined in the included studies reflects platform popularity and research trends at the time of data collection.
As a result, some widely used platforms are overrepresented (e.g., Facebook and Instagram), whereas others remain underexamined.
This imbalance limits the generalizability of platform-level comparisons.
Third, a focus on platforms alone may obscure the active role of users in shaping their experiences.
Platform-level analyses cannot fully capture the dynamic interactions between platform features, individual characteristics, and usage practices (40).
text.formatted: Platform-level analyses cannot fully capture the dynamic interactions between platform features, individual characteristics, and usage practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(40)</ref>.

text.text: In conclusion, the cross-platform perspective represents a promising and informative direction for research on SNS use and mental health, provided that it is theoretically grounded, methodologically rigorous, and oriented toward the identification of underlying platform characteristics rather than platforms themselves.
